1.title: Know the words of bookkeeping
1.intro: Bookkeeping is recording money in and out so that a business can see where it stands.
pts: Learn the terms: asset, liability, equity, income, expense, debit, credit, ledger, invoice, receipt.
Assets are what a business has; liabilities are what it owes; equity is what is left.
Every entry has two sides: a debit and a credit that are equal.
Bookkeepers record; accountants and tax advisers give advice. Know the difference.
1.ex: The business buys a printer for 300 cash. Debit equipment 300, credit cash 300.
1.act: Write ten terms with an example each and sort 15 transactions into income or expense.
1.std: Task: sort and define. Condition: from a list, no help. Standard: all terms plain and correct and 15 of 15 transactions sorted.

2.title: Explain the books from receipt to report
2.intro: The books follow a path. If you can name it, you can keep it tidy.
pts: The path: collect documents, record, categorise, reconcile, review, report.
A chart of accounts is the list of categories used for all entries.
Reconcile means compare your books to the bank statement and explain each difference.
Keep a file for every document: receipts, invoices, bank statements.
2.ex: Bank balance 1,200; books 1,050. A cheque for 150 has not cleared. Books plus outstanding adjustment match.
2.act: Set up a chart of accounts for a small shop and trace five transactions through it.
2.std: Task: trace five transactions. Condition: using a sheet or free practice file. Standard: each entry is balanced and has a document.

3.title: Record and reconcile to a standard
3.intro: Now you do the work. Enter a month of transactions and prove the books agree with the bank.
pts: Enter income and expenses with the date, who, what, amount and tax.
Categorise the same way each time.
Reconcile the bank each month; list every difference and fix it.
Produce a simple profit and loss and a list of who owes the business and whom it owes.
3.ex: A month: income 4,200, expenses 3,100, profit 1,100. Bank reconciled with zero unexplained difference.
3.act: Complete one month of practice books and a reconciliation.
3.std: Task: complete one month of books. Condition: from provided documents in three hours. Standard: debits equal credits, bank reconciled, and reports show a correct profit.

4.title: Follow Canadian tax and record rules
4.intro: Canadian businesses have sales tax, payroll and record rules. Learn where they touch the books.
pts: GST/HST and some provincial sales taxes may apply; registration depends on sales and rules. Check the current limits and rates with the tax agency.
If a business pays staff, it must withhold and send deductions to the tax agency by their due dates. Check the current rules.
Business records are generally kept for six years; check the current rule.
Keep client information private and give tax or legal advice only if you are qualified. Professional titles for accountants are protected; use only titles you hold.
4.ex: A client asks if a car expense is fully deductible. You say you will note it and refer the question to a tax professional.
4.act: Make a table of tax or record item, who sets it, due date and where you checked, for ten items.
4.std: Task: build a tax and records table. Condition: using official public pages. Standard: each row has a dated source and unclear items say 'check the current rule with the local authority'.

5.title: Price your bookkeeping and check it pays
5.intro: You are paid for accuracy and time. Work out what each client really costs you.
pts: Time includes collecting documents, chasing missing items, entering, reconciling and questions.
Compare hourly, monthly fixed fee and per-transaction pricing.
A fixed fee needs a clear scope: number of transactions, accounts and reports.
Track hours per client to see if the fee is fair.
5.ex: A client has 80 transactions a month. It takes 3 hours at 40 USD an hour: 120 USD a month. Teaching figures only.
5.act: Time three practice clients and set a monthly fee for each.
5.std: Task: price three clients. Condition: from your time log. Standard: hours, rate and fee are shown and a mentor can follow every number.

6.title: Use software and find clients
6.intro: Software saves time. Clients come from trust.
pts: Use accounting software with a bank feed and a clear audit trail; practise on a demo file.
Check each automated entry. The software suggests, you decide.
Reach local small businesses, with consent, and offer a free 20-minute review of their record keeping.
Ask permission before using any client example, and remove names.
6.ex: The bank feed suggests 'office' for a grocery bill. You change it to 'meals' after checking the receipt.
6.act: Practise software on a demo file and contact ten small businesses.
6.std: Task: practise and reach out. Condition: demo data and consent-based contact. Standard: ten entries checked, ten contacts made and replies logged.

7.title: Protect clients, data and accuracy
pts: Keep client files in a secure place with strong passwords and two-step sign-in.
Back up data and test that you can restore it.
Use a second check on large or unusual payments.
Write an engagement letter that lists scope, fees, deadlines, who is responsible for what and how you keep information private.
7.ex: Your letter says: 'The client provides all documents by the 10th. The bookkeeper reconciles by the 20th.'
7.act: Write an engagement letter and a monthly close checklist.
7.std: Task: produce a letter and checklist. Condition: reviewed by a mentor. Standard: scope, fees, deadlines and privacy are stated in plain words.

8.title: Run a real bookkeeping practice for 60 days
8.intro: Now you run it, measure and decide.
pts: Set a goal such as two clients and two monthly closes.
Each week record hours, income, errors found and late items.
Ask each client for feedback.
Choose at the end: stop, change or grow, and write a 12-month plan.
8.ex: After 60 days: 2 clients, 14 hours, 560 USD, no unexplained bank differences. You plan to add a third client.
8.act: Run the pilot and present a 12-month plan to a panel of three.
8.std: Task: run a 60-day pilot. Condition: real or practice clients with a signed letter. Standard: log complete, reconciliations clean and the decision uses numbers.

quiz: What are assets, liabilities and equity?
What a business has, what it owes, and what is left.
What does every entry have?
A debit and an equal credit.
What is a reconciliation?
Comparing the books to the bank and explaining each difference.
What is a chart of accounts?
The list of categories used for entries.
How long are business records generally kept?
Generally six years; check the current rule.
Who decides when the software suggests a category?
The bookkeeper.
What does an engagement letter list?
Scope, fees, deadlines, responsibilities and privacy.
Why test a restore?
A backup you have not tested may not work.
When should you refer a tax question?
When it needs advice from a qualified tax professional.
What do you do when you do not know a rule?
Check the current rule with the local authority.
